$$M:=\sup_{s\in[x-a,x+a]}|u''''(s)|<+\infty .$$

Then

$$\left|\frac{u(x+a)-2u(x)+u(x-a)}{a^2}-u''(x)\right|\le\frac{M\,a^2}{12}.$$

Use the notation $z_{j+N}=z_j$, $(D_+z)_j=(z_{j+1}-z_j)/a$, $(\Delta_az)_j=(z_{j+1}-2z_j+z_{j-1})/a^2$, $\langle z,w\rangle_a=a\sum_jz_jw_j$, $\|z\|_a^2=\langle z,z\rangle_a$ and $E_a(q,p)=\tfrac12(\|p\|_a^2+c^2\|D_+q\|_a^2)$ of [[def-cm-cyclic-spring-chain]].

**(a) Summation by parts.** For all $z,w\in\mathbb R^N$,

$$\langle D_+z,D_+w\rangle_a=-\langle \Delta_az,w\rangle_a .$$

**(b) Scaled Cauchy-Schwarz.** For all $z,w\in\mathbb R^N$, $|\langle z,w\rangle_a|\le\|z\|_a\|w\|_a$ ([[prop-coordinate-cauchy-schwarz-agrees-with-the-finite-sum-theorem]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(c) Energy identity.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $q:I\to\mathbb R^N$ be $C^2$ and let $R:I\to\mathbb R^N$ be continuous with

$$q_j''=\frac{c^2}{a^2}\bigl(q_{j+1}-2q_j+q_{j-1}\bigr)+R_j=c^2(\Delta_aq)_j+R_j\qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N).$$

Then $t\mapsto E_a(q(t),q'(t))$ is $C^1$ on $I$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}E_a\bigl(q(t),q'(t)\bigr)=a\sum_{j=1}^N R_j(t)\,q_j'(t),$$

and consequently $\bigl|\frac{d}{dt}E_a\bigr|\le\|R(t)\|_a\,\sqrt{2E_a(t)}$ whenever $E_a\ge0$ (which always holds).

For $a,b\in\mathbb R^n$, Cauchy–Schwarz in the standard coordinate inner product is exactly

$$\left|\sum_{k<n}a_kb_k\right|\le\sqrt{\sum_{k<n}a_k^2}\sqrt{\sum_{k<n}b_k^2},$$

with equality exactly when the two lists are proportional in the symmetric sense. This includes $n=0$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]), and suppose

$$f(a) \;=\; f(b) .$$

Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with $f'(c) = 0$.

**Three hypotheses, three different jobs.** Continuity on the **closed**
interval is what the extreme value theorem consumes; differentiability on the
**open** interval is what Fermat's theorem consumes, and it is asked for
nowhere else; and $f(a) = f(b)$ is what forces the extremum inside when neither
extremum is attained in the interior. Continuity at the two endpoints cannot be
dropped, and a false statement later on this page records a witness for that.

**Differentiability is meant with respect to the domain $[a,b]$.** For $c$ in
the open interval that is the same condition as differentiability of any
restriction of $f$ to a subinterval around $c$, since only points near $c$
enter, but the phrase is fixed here so that the citation of
[[thm-fermat-interior-extremum]], whose hypothesis is interiority in the
domain, is exact.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $N\ge2$ be an integer, let $a>0$ and $c>0$ be real parameters, and let $L:=Na$. Indices are read modulo $N$: $z_{j+N}:=z_j$.

**(a) The chain.** A **state of the chain** is a pair $(q,p)\in\mathbb R^N\times\mathbb R^N$, where $q=(q_1,\dots,q_N)$ are the positions and $p=(q_1',\dots,q_N')$ the velocities of the $N$ nodes. The **cyclic spring-chain system** is the first-order system

$$q_j'=p_j,\qquad p_j'=\frac{c^2}{a^2}\bigl(q_{j+1}-2q_j+q_{j-1}\bigr)\qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N),$$

equivalently the second-order system $q_j''=\frac{c^2}{a^2}(q_{j+1}-2q_j+q_{j-1})$ for a $C^2$ curve $q:I\to\mathbb R^N$. Its **discrete energy** is

$$E(q,p):=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^N\Bigl(p_j^2+\frac{c^2}{a^2}\bigl(q_{j+1}-q_j\bigr)^2\Bigr).$$

**(b) Discrete norms and differences.** For $z,w\in\mathbb R^N$ define the **scaled inner product and norm**

$$\langle z,w\rangle_a:=a\sum_{j=1}^N z_jw_j,\qquad \|z\|_a:=\langle z,z\rangle_a^{1/2},$$

and for the discrete difference $(D_+z)_j:=(z_{j+1}-z_j)/a$. The **discrete Laplacian** is $(\Delta_az)_j:=(z_{j+1}-2z_j+z_{j-1})/a^2$.

**(c) The comparison class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a function that is $C^2$ in the first variable and $C^4$ in the second, is $L$-periodic in $x$ ($u(t,x+L)=u(t,x)$ for all $(t,x)$), and satisfies

$$u_{tt}(t,x)=c^2u_{xx}(t,x)\qquad\bigl((t,x)\in I\times\mathbb R\bigr).$$

For a compact subinterval $[0,T]\subseteq I$ put $M_T:=\sup\{|\partial_x^4u(t,x)|:(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb R\}$ (finite when continuous derivatives are bounded on the compact time interval, as assumed in the items that use it), and for $a=L/N$ define the **sampled initial data**

$$q_j(0):=u(0,ja),\qquad q_j'(0):=u_t(0,ja)\qquad(j=1,\dots,N).$$

For $a,b\in\mathbb R^n$, Cauchy–Schwarz in the standard coordinate inner product is exactly

$$\left|\sum_{k<n}a_kb_k\right|\le\sqrt{\sum_{k<n}a_k^2}\sqrt{\sum_{k<n}b_k^2},$$

with equality exactly when the two lists are proportional in the symmetric sense. This includes $n=0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

derivations.claim: Write the chain as the first-order system $z'=Bz$ on $\mathbb R^{2N}$ with $z=(q,p)$ and the constant matrix $B(q,p)=(p,\frac{c^2}{a^2}(q_{j+1}-2q_j+q_{j-1}))_j$. By [F1] applied to the matrix ODE with $C(t)=B$ on $[-1,T+1]$ and initial time $0$, the initial value problem $z'=Bz$, $z(0)=(q(0),q'(0))$ has a unique solution on $[0,T]$, and its first component is the unique solution $q$ of the chain equations with the sampled data. The solution is smooth on the larger interval by repeated differentiation of its constant-coefficient equation. Restricting to $[0,T]$ proves (i), including $T=0$; in that case all errors and energy at $0$ vanish by the sampled state and every bound is immediate.

Put $u_j(t):=u(t,ja)$ and define $$R_j(t):=c^2\bigl(\Delta_au_j(t)-u_{xx}(t,ja)\bigr)=c^2\Delta_au_j(t)-u_{tt}(t,ja),$$ the last equality by $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$. By [F2], $|R_j(t)|\le c^2Ma^2/12$ for every $j,t$, hence $$\|R(t)\|_a=\Bigl(a\sum_jR_j(t)^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\frac{c^2Ma^2}{12}\sqrt{aN}=Ca^2 .$$ Since $e_j=q_j-u_j$, the identities $u_j''=c^2(\Delta_au)_j-R_j$ and $q_j''=c^2(\Delta_aq)_j$ give $e_j''=c^2(\Delta_ae)_j+R_j$; moreover $e_j(0)=0$ and $e_j'(0)=0$ by the sampled initial data.

Put $E_a(t):=\tfrac12(\|e'(t)\|_a^2+c^2\|D_+e(t)\|_a^2)$, which is $\ge0$ with $E_a(0)=0$. By [F3] (the energy identity with the perturbation $R$ of step 2.1), $$\frac{d}{dt}\sqrt{2E_a(t)+\delta}=\frac{E_a'(t)}{\sqrt{2E_a(t)+\delta}}\le\frac{\|R(t)\|_a\sqrt{2E_a(t)}}{\sqrt{2E_a(t)+\delta}}\le\|R(t)\|_a\le Ca^2$$ for every $\delta>0$. Integrating from $0$ and letting $\delta\downarrow0$ gives $\sqrt{2E_a(t)}\le Ca^2t$; in particular $\|e'(t)\|_a\le Ca^2t$. Integrating $e(t)=e(0)+\int_0^te'(s)ds$ and using [F5] gives $\|e(t)\|_a\le\int_0^tCs a^2ds=\tfrac12Ca^2t^2$. This is (ii).

By [F5], $\max_j|e_j(t)|\le a^{-1/2}\|e(t)\|_a\le\tfrac12Ca^{3/2}t^2$, which is (iii). For (iv), fix $t\in[0,T]$ and $x=ja+s$ with $0\le s\le a$. The interpolant of the samples of $u$ satisfies the chord bound [F4] on $[ja,(j+1)a]$ with $\varphi=u(t,\cdot)$, and $|I_aq(t,x)-I_au(t,x)|\le\max_j|e_j(t)|$ because both interpolations are convex combinations of their nodal values; hence $$\sup_{x}\bigl|I_aq(t,x)-u(t,x)\bigr|\le\max_j|e_j(t)|+\frac{M_2a^2}{8}.$$ By (iii) the right-hand side tends to $0$ as $a\to0$ uniformly on $[0,T]$.

citations.quote:
Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

**Why this item is first.** The published definition of the integral does not
cover this page. [[def-darboux-integral]] is stated for reals $a < b$, because
the partitions it quantifies over are those of [[def-partition-and-refinement]],
whose standing hypothesis is $a < b$: with $a = b$ the chain
$a = t_0 < \dots < t_n = b$ is unsatisfiable. So $\int_a^b f$ is an undefined
symbol whenever $a \ge b$, and every additivity statement below would be
ill-formed as it is usually written. This item extends the notation, and nothing
else: the object it names is still the Darboux integral of
[[def-darboux-integral]].

Let $u, v \in \mathbb{R}$ and write

$$[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v] \;:=\; \text{the closed interval with endpoints } u \text{ and } v$$

([[def-interval]]). Let $f$ be a real-valued function whose domain contains that
interval. Say that **$f$ is integrable between $u$ and $v$** when either $u = v$,
or $u \ne v$ and the restriction of $f$ to $[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v]$ is bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux integrable there ([[def-darboux-integral]],
[[def-darboux-sums]]). For such $f$ define

$$\int_u^v f \;:=\; \begin{cases} \text{the Darboux integral of } f \text{ over } [u,v] & \text{if } u < v, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } u = v, \\[2pt] -\displaystyle\int_v^u f & \text{if } u > v. \end{cases}$$

**There is nothing to check for consistency.** The three clauses are indexed by
the three cases of trichotomy, $u < v$, $u = v$ and $u > v$, which are mutually
exclusive and exhaustive; no pair of them ever applies to the same $(u,v)$. In
particular the first clause is untouched, so on $u < v$ this is the published
integral verbatim and every published theorem about it applies unchanged.

**The middle clause is a stipulation, not a computation.** It is *not* claimed
that $0$ is a value forced by the $u < v$ definition in any limiting sense; that
definition simply says nothing at $u = v$, and $\int_u^u f := 0$ is what is
written there. It is also unconditional: no hypothesis on $f$ beyond being
defined at $u$ is asked for, since the case $u = v$ never refers to a partition.

### The two consequences used throughout the page

**Antisymmetry, for every pair.** For all reals $u, v$ with $f$ integrable
between them,

$$\int_u^v f \;=\; -\int_v^u f .$$

Indeed if $u < v$ then $v > u$ and the third clause reads
$\int_v^u f = -\int_u^v f$, which rearranges to the display; if $u = v$ both
sides are $0$; and if $u > v$ the third clause is the display itself.

**Absolute values agree.** Consequently
$\bigl|\int_u^v f\bigr| = \bigl|\int_v^u f\bigr|$ for every such pair.

**An obligation recorded here and discharged elsewhere.** With this convention
the additivity identity

$$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f$$

holds for **every** arrangement of $u, v, w$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable, not only for $u < v < w$. That is a theorem and not part of this
definition; it is proved as the last clause of
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], and nothing on this page uses it before it
is proved there.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $k,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be an injective $C^k$ map whose derivative is invertible everywhere. Then $f[U]$ is open and the corestriction $f:U\to f[U]$ is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and equals $Df(a)v$. In particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ is $Jf(a)$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

derivations.claim: Fix $t\in[0,T_0)$. If $a<b$ and $\varphi_t(a)=\varphi_t(b)$, then $b-a=-t(f(b)-f(a))\le tK(b-a)<b-a$ by [F1] and $tK<1$, a contradiction; hence $\varphi_t$ is injective. Moreover $\varphi_t(a)=a+tf(a)\to\pm\infty$ as $a\to\pm\infty$ because $f$ is bounded and $a\to\pm\infty$; by [F2] it is surjective. Finally $\varphi_t'(a)=1+tf'(a)\ge1-tK>0$, so [F2] makes $\varphi_t$ a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto $\mathbb R$.

Endpoint level set. Let $F_0(a):=a+T_0f(a)$. Its derivative is $1+T_0f'(a)\ge0$, so [F1] makes it nondecreasing. Since $f$ is bounded, $F_0(a)\to\pm\infty$ as $a\to\pm\infty$. Its level set $S=F_0^{-1}(x_*)$ is therefore a nonempty compact interval $[\alpha,\beta]$, containing $a_*$. If $\alpha<\beta$, then $F_0$ is constant on this interval, so $f'=-K$ in its interior and, by continuity, at its endpoints. If $\alpha=\beta=a_*$ the same derivative value follows from the hypothesis. Thus $f'=-K$ on all of $S$.

Fix $(t_0,x_0)$ with $0\le t_0<T_0$ and put $a_0:=a(t_0,x_0)$. By step 1.1, $1+t_0f'(a_0)>0$. Continuity gives an open rectangle $Q$ around $(t_0,a_0)$ on which $1+tf'(a)>0$. For each fixed $t$ in this rectangle, [F4] shows that $a\mapsto\varphi_t(a)$ is strictly increasing on its $a$-interval. Thus $\Phi(t,a):=(t,\varphi_t(a))$ is injective on $Q$, and its derivative has determinant $1+tf'(a)>0$. The injective-regular corollary therefore makes $\Phi|_Q$ a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto its open image. This also applies at $t_0=0$, because $Q$ may extend to small negative times and the determinant remains positive locally. On the portion with $t\ge0$, the local inverse agrees with the globally defined $a(t,x)=\varphi_t^{-1}(x)$ by uniqueness of the inverse. Hence $a(t,x)$ is $C^1$ in a relative neighbourhood of every point of $[0,T_0)\times\mathbb R$, and differentiating the identity $\varphi_t(a(t,x))=x$ is now legitimate: $$\partial_xa(t,x)=\frac{1}{1+tf'(a(t,x))},\qquad \partial_ta(t,x)=-\frac{f(a(t,x))}{1+tf'(a(t,x))}.$$ By [F3], $u=f\circ a$ is $C^1$ jointly, $u(0,x)=f(x)$, and $$u_t=-f'(a)\frac{f(a)}{1+tf'(a)},\qquad u_x=\frac{f'(a)}{1+tf'(a)},\qquad u_t+u\,u_x=\frac{f'(a)}{1+tf'(a)}\bigl(-f(a)+f(a)\bigr)=0 .$$ This proves (i).

Label limit. The identity $a(t)+tf(a(t))=x_*$ and boundedness of $f$ keep $a(t)$ in a fixed compact interval. Every subsequential limit $a_0$ as $t\to T_0$ from below satisfies $F_0(a_0)=x_*$, hence belongs to $S$. For $a\in S$, $f(a)=K(x_*-a)$, so $\varphi_t(a)=(1-tK)a+tKx_*$. If $x_*<\alpha$, this gives $\varphi_t(\alpha)>x_*$ and strict monotonicity of $\varphi_t$ from step 1.1 forces $a(t)<\alpha$; its only possible limit in $S$ is $\alpha$. Similarly, if $x_*>\beta$, $a(t)>\beta$ and its only possible limit in $S$ is $\beta$. If $x_*\in S$, then $f(x_*)=0$ and $\varphi_t(x_*)=x_*$, so uniqueness of the inverse gives $a(t)=x_*$. Thus every subsequential limit as $t\to T_0$ from below equals $a^\dagger$. If $a(t)$ did not converge to $a^\dagger$, there would be $\varepsilon>0$ and a sequence $t_m\to T_0$ from below with $|a(t_m)-a^\dagger|\ge\varepsilon$. Boundedness and [F5] give a convergent subsequence of labels, contradicting the identified limit. Therefore $a(t)\to a^\dagger$, and by step 1.2 and continuity, $f'(a(t))\to-K$.

Fix $a_0\in\mathbb R$ and put $x(t):=\varphi_t(a_0)=a_0+tf(a_0)$; then $a(t,x(t))=a_0$, so $u(t,x(t))=f(a_0)$ is constant. By step 2.1, $q(t)=u_x(t,x(t))=f'(a_0)/(1+tf'(a_0))$, and differentiating this quotient with [F3], $$q'(t)=-\frac{f'(a_0)^2}{(1+tf'(a_0))^2}=-q(t)^2 .$$ This proves (ii).

Fixed-spatial gradient blow-up. Step 2.1 gives $u_x(t,x_*)=f'(a(t))/(1+tf'(a(t)))$. Its denominator is positive for $t<T_0$ by step 1.1 and tends to $1-T_0K=0$, while its numerator tends to $-K\ne0$ by step 2.2. Hence $|u_x(t,x_*)|\to+\infty$, and the supremum over $x$ diverges as well. Also $|u(t,x_*)|=|f(a(t))|\le\|f\|_\infty$. Independently, along the specified characteristic $\varphi_t(a_*)$, step 3.1 gives $u_x(t,\varphi_t(a_*))=-K/(1-tK)$. Thus the fixed-spatial and material-characteristic gradient blow-up claims both hold even when the endpoint map has a flat level interval; no injectivity at $T_0$ was assumed.

risk_review.notes: Bounded f and f prime>=-K give onto strictly increasing characteristic maps before T0=1/K. Open-rectangle inverse argument proves joint C1 even at t=0. Endpoint F0 is nondecreasing and coercive; compact level interval has f prime=-K, including a singleton by the specified a*. Labels remain bounded and all subsequential limits equal the clamp of x* to this interval, giving fixed-space denominator->0 positive, numerator->-K. citations.quote:
Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the actual Lebesgue measure foundation used by the bounded Borel weak/entropy class.

Write $F(u):=\tfrac12u^2$ and let $\lambda_2$ be two-dimensional Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^2$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]).

Every space-time expression written as $\int_0^\infty\!\!\int_{\mathbb R}(\cdots)\,dx\,dt$ below means the single signed Lebesgue integral over $[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with respect to $\lambda_2$; it is not an iterated-integral convention. The initial-data integral is with respect to one-dimensional Lebesgue measure $\lambda_1$. In (W) and (E), each integrand is Borel measurable, bounded, and supported in the compact support of the test function (or its initial trace). A compact support is contained in a bounded rectangle of finite Lebesgue measure, by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]; monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral give $\int |q|\le\|q\|_\infty\lambda_d(K)<\infty$ for such an integrand $q$ supported in $K$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Thus all displayed signed integrals are defined as Lebesgue integrals of integrable functions ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]).

A **test function** is a function $\varphi:[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^1$ up to the boundary: it is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open neighborhood of this closed half-space, and its support within the half-space is compact. No vanishing or continuation by zero for $t<0$ is required. Thus the trace $\varphi(0,x)$ may be nonzero. Derivatives at $t=0$ are the continuous one-sided derivatives. Write $C_c^1([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R)$ for this class; **admissible** means belonging to this class and **nonnegative** means $\varphi\ge0$ on the half-space.

**(a) Weak solutions.** Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and Borel measurable ([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]) and let $u:(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and Borel measurable. Then $u$ is a **weak solution of**

$$u_t+\bigl(F(u)\bigr)_x=0 \qquad\text{with }u(0,\cdot)=f \tag{CL}$$

when

$$\int_0^\infty\!\!\int_{\mathbb R}\Bigl[u(t,x)\varphi_t(t,x)+F\bigl(u(t,x)\bigr)\varphi_x(t,x)\Bigr]dx\,dt+\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\varphi(0,x)\,dx=0 \tag{W}$$

for every test function $\varphi$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). The integrals exist because $u,f$ are bounded and the test functions have compact support; the identity depends on $u$ and $f$ only through their almost-everywhere classes.

**(b) Entropy pairs.** An **entropy pair** is a pair $(\eta,q)$ of $C^1$ functions $\eta,q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-derivative]]) such that

$$q'(u)=\eta'(u)\,F'(u)=u\,\eta'(u)\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R;$$

the function $\eta$ is then called an **entropy** and $q$ its **entropy flux**. The entropy is **convex** when $\eta((1-a)r+as)\le(1-a)\eta(r)+a\eta(s)$ for all real $r,s$ and $a\in[0,1]$.

**(c) Entropy solutions.** A weak solution $u$ of (CL) is an **entropy solution** when, for every convex entropy pair $(\eta,q)$ with $q'=u\eta'$, the distributional inequality

$$\bigl(\eta(u)\bigr)_t+\bigl(q(u)\bigr)_x\le0$$

holds, by definition meaning that

$$\int_0^\infty\!\!\int_{\mathbb R}\Bigl[\eta\bigl(u\bigr)\varphi_t+q\bigl(u\bigr)\varphi_x\Bigr]dx\,dt+\int_{\mathbb R}\eta\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\varphi(0,x)\,dx\ \ge\ 0 \tag{E}$$

for every nonnegative test function $\varphi$.

**(d) Riemann data.** For reals $u_L,u_R$ the **Riemann initial data** are

$$f(x):=\begin{cases}u_L,&x<0,\\ u_R,&x\ge0.\end{cases}$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: On each of the two open regions $x<st$ and $x>st$ the function $u$ of (a) is constant, so the equation holds classically there. The traces across $x=st$ are $u_-=u_L$ (left) and $u_+=u_R$ (right), and the initial trace is the Riemann data $f$. By [F1], the weak residual of (a) integrates $\varphi(t,st)$ against $$s[u]-[F(u)]=s(u_R-u_L)-\tfrac12(u_R^2-u_L^2)=(u_R-u_L)\Bigl(s-\frac{u_L+u_R}{2}\Bigr)=0 .$$ Hence the weak identity (W) holds for every test function, and $u$ is a weak solution.

For (c), first integrate on $\varepsilon<t<T$, splitting the truncated domain into the left constant region, the fan, and the right constant region, with $T$ and the spatial cutoff outside the support of the test function. There $u=x/t$ is $C^1$ on the closed fan and satisfies $u_t+uu_x=0$ by [F3]; the constant pieces do too. Apply the divergence theorem to each piece. On a shared fan edge the outward normals are opposite and the traces of $u$, $F(u)$ and $\varphi$ agree, so the two boundary integrals cancel. The bottom term is $-\int u(\varepsilon,x)\varphi(\varepsilon,x)\,dx$. As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, $u(\varepsilon,x)$ differs from $f(x)$ only between the rays $x=u_L\varepsilon$ and $x=u_R\varepsilon$, an interval of length $(u_R-u_L)\varepsilon$, and it is uniformly bounded by $\max(|u_L|,|u_R|)$. Thus the difference in the bottom integral tends to zero; continuity of $\varphi$ on its compact support replaces $\varphi(\varepsilon,x)$ by $\varphi(0,x)$. The integrands over $0<t<\varepsilon$ are bounded on a fixed compact spatial support, so their integrals also tend to zero. Taking the limit gives (W) with the actual initial term.

For (b), apply the same computation to the pair $(\eta_k,q_k)$ in place of $(u,F(u))$: on each open region the function $u$ is constant, so $(\eta_k(u))_t+(q_k(u))_x=0$ classically there, and [F1] gives $$\int_0^\infty\!\!\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl[\eta_k\varphi_t+q_k\varphi_x\bigr]+\int_{\mathbb R}\eta_k(f)\varphi(0)=\int_0^\infty\varphi(t,st)\bigl(s[\eta_k]-[q_k]\bigr)dt .$$ For $u_R<k<u_L$ a direct evaluation gives $[\eta_k]=2k-u_L-u_R$ and $[q_k]=(2k^2-u_L^2-u_R^2)/2$, whence $s[\eta_k]-[q_k]=-(k-u_L)(k-u_R)\ge0$. For $k\ge u_L$ or $k\le u_R$ the same expressions give $s[\eta_k]-[q_k]=0$. In every case the right-hand side is $\ge0$ for nonnegative test functions, which is (E).

Let $(\eta,q)$ be any convex $C^1$ entropy pair. On either side of the shock the entropy residual vanishes classically, and [F1] applied to $(\eta(u),q(u))$ gives the residual coefficient $$s[\eta]-[q]=\int_{u_R}^{u_L}(z-s)\eta'(z)\,dz=\int_{u_R}^{u_L}(z-s)\bigl(\eta'(z)-\eta'(s)\bigr)\,dz\ge0.$$ The middle equality uses $s=(u_L+u_R)/2$, hence $\int_{u_R}^{u_L}(z-s)dz=0$. For any $a<b$, convexity gives $\eta(a+h)\le(1-h/(b-a))\eta(a)+(h/(b-a))\eta(b)$ for $0<h<b-a$; dividing by $h$ after subtracting $\eta(a)$ and taking $h\downarrow0$ yields $\eta'(a)\le(\eta(b)-\eta(a))/(b-a)$. Applying convexity to $b-h$ and taking the same limit gives $(\eta(b)-\eta(a))/(b-a)\le\eta'(b)$. Thus $\eta'$ is nondecreasing, so $(z-s)(\eta'(z)-\eta'(s))\ge0$ for every $z$. This proves (E) for every declared convex $C^1$ pair, in addition to the Kružkov computation of step 2.1.

On the rarefaction fan every $C^1$ entropy pair has $\partial_t\eta(u)+\partial_xq(u)=\eta'(u)(u_t+uu_x)=0$; its traces are continuous across the fan edges. For a Kružkov pair split additionally along $x=kt$ when that line lies inside the fan; the two entropy and flux traces agree there too. Apply the truncated-domain argument of step 1.2 to these entropy fields. Since $u$ ranges in the compact interval $[u_L,u_R]$, $\eta(u)$ and $q(u)$ are bounded and the initial difference is supported on an interval of length $(u_R-u_L)\varepsilon$; the same limit establishes (E) with equality and its nonzero initial trace for every stated pair. Both profiles are therefore entropy solutions for the full class of the Definition, with the asserted additional Kružkov identities.

Step 2.1 gives coefficient zero for k outside [uR,uL] and at either endpoint; zero left or right state is allowed provided their strict ordering holds.

risk_review.notes: Interface outward normals (s,-1) on right and (-s,1) on left give coefficient s[u]-[F]. Shock speed cancels weak residual; Kruzhkov residual is -(k-uL)(k-uR) inside and zero outside including endpoints. Convex C1 derivative monotonicity proved with secant inequalities makes general entropy coefficient nonnegative. Fan truncation t>=epsilon permits C1 divergence and continuous trace cancellation; shrinking initial discrepancy has length (uR-uL)epsilon, bounded integrands give convergence. Entropy kink line also has equal traces; no false smoothness at apex assumed. Exact weak definition and divergence suppliers checked.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, let $\chi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$ and material derivative $D_t$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]], [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]), and let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$. Define the swept region $\Sigma=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$.

Write $\mathcal D_\chi:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}$ for the open domain of the spatial velocity $u$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), and take $U\subseteq\mathcal D_\chi$ open and containing $\Sigma$. Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be a $C^1$ density field, let $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^1$ field (the stress field of [[def-cm-traction-and-stress]]), and let $b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Suppose:

**(K)** $\rho$ satisfies $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ at every $(t,x)$ with $t\in J_0$ and $x\in\chi_t(B)$;

**(L)** for every material subregion $B'$ (nonempty bounded open with $\overline{B'}\subseteq B$) and every $t\in J_0$ for which $\chi_t(B')$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) , the balance is

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)u(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)b(t,x)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(B')}\sigma(t,y)\,\nu(y)\,dS(y),$$

where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal and the surface integral is that of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]].

Define the **row divergence** of $\sigma$ componentwise by

$$g(t,x):=\Bigl(\sum_{j}\partial_j\sigma_{1j},\ \sum_{j}\partial_j\sigma_{2j},\ \sum_{j}\partial_j\sigma_{3j}\Bigr)(t,x).$$

Then for every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$,

$$\rho(t,x)\,D_tu(t,x)=\rho(t,x)\,b(t,x)+g(t,x).$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $u:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ spatial velocity field with the conventions of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]. Write $Du(t,x)$ for the total derivative in the spatial variable and $\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{tr}(Du)$ ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**(a) Incompressible Newtonian fluid.** Model data are a $C^1$ scalar field $p:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ (**pressure**) and a real number $\eta>0$ (**dynamic viscosity**; a dimensionless mathematical parameter until a unit system is fixed). The model consists of the **incompressibility constraint**

$$\operatorname{div}u(t,x)=0\qquad\bigl((t,x)\in I\times O\bigr)$$

and the **Newtonian stress field**

$$\sigma(t,x):=-p(t,x)I_3+\eta\bigl(Du(t,x)+Du(t,x)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$

with $Du^{\mathsf T}$ the transpose and $I_3$ the identity ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], [[def-matrix-space]]). The second term is symmetric, so $\sigma$ is symmetric for every $(t,x)$.

**(b) Barotropic inviscid fluid.** Model data are a $C^1$ function $p:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ (**pressure law**) and a $C^1$ **potential** $V:I\times O\to\mathbb R$. The **enthalpy** of the pressure law is the $C^1$ function

$$h(\rho):=\int_1^\rho\frac{p'(s)}{s}\,ds\qquad(\rho>0),$$

which is characterised by $h(1)=0$ and $h'(\rho)=p'(\rho)/\rho$ for every $\rho>0$ ([[def-the-integral-function]], [[thm-ftc-first-part]]). For a $C^1$ positive density field $\rho:I\times O\to(0,\infty)$ the branch's stress field is

$$\sigma(t,x):=-p\bigl(\rho(t,x)\bigr)I_3 ,$$

and the branch is **inviscid** (no velocity-gradient term) and **barotropic** (the stress depends on position and time only through the density).

Throughout, $\mathbb R^3$ carries its standard ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$, its Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $a\in O$ and let $v:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that the total derivative $Dv(a):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is a linear map ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) whose matrix in the standard bases is $\bigl(\partial_jv_i(a)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le3}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is

$$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Dv(a)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$

the trace of the total derivative ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]), read in the standard basis of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]).

For a $C^1$ scalar field $f:O\to\mathbb R$ and $a\in O$, the **gradient** $\nabla f(a)\in\mathbb R^3$ is the vector of partial derivatives of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; it is the unique vector with $Df(a)h=\langle\nabla f(a),h\rangle_2$ for every $h\in\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). We write $\langle\nabla f(a),v(a)\rangle_2=:\nabla f(a)\cdot v(a)$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $f:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For $(t,x)\in I\times O$ write $D_x f(t,x):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ for the total derivative of $y\mapsto f(t,y)$ at fixed $t$, and $\nabla_xf(t,x)$ for its gradient. The derivative $Df(t,x)$ of the full map on $I\times O$ acts on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$; it is distinct from $D_x f$. Define the partial time derivative $\partial_tf(t,x):=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=t}f(s,x)$ and the **material derivative** of $f$ along $u$

$$D_tf(t,x):=\partial_tf(t,x)+D_xf(t,x)\bigl(u(t,x)\bigr)=\partial_tf(t,x)+\nabla_x f(t,x)\cdot u(t,x).$$

Spatial derivatives $Du$, $Dw$, $\nabla f$ and $\operatorname{div}u$ of time-dependent fields always mean $D_xu$, $D_xw$, $\nabla_x f$ and spatial divergence at fixed time; a stationary field $u(x)$ is included by setting $u(t,x)=u(x)$. The same definitions apply on any open spacetime domain, by restriction to a product neighborhood of each point.

For a $C^1$ vector field $w:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ the material derivative $D_tw$ is defined componentwise, and $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)$ means the divergence of $x\mapsto w(t,x)$ at $x$ at each fixed $t$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and equals $Df(a)v$. In particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ is $Jf(a)$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

**Why this item is first.** The published definition of the integral does not
cover this page. [[def-darboux-integral]] is stated for reals $a < b$, because
the partitions it quantifies over are those of [[def-partition-and-refinement]],
whose standing hypothesis is $a < b$: with $a = b$ the chain
$a = t_0 < \dots < t_n = b$ is unsatisfiable. So $\int_a^b f$ is an undefined
symbol whenever $a \ge b$, and every additivity statement below would be
ill-formed as it is usually written. This item extends the notation, and nothing
else: the object it names is still the Darboux integral of
[[def-darboux-integral]].

Let $u, v \in \mathbb{R}$ and write

$$[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v] \;:=\; \text{the closed interval with endpoints } u \text{ and } v$$

([[def-interval]]). Let $f$ be a real-valued function whose domain contains that
interval. Say that **$f$ is integrable between $u$ and $v$** when either $u = v$,
or $u \ne v$ and the restriction of $f$ to $[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v]$ is bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux integrable there ([[def-darboux-integral]],
[[def-darboux-sums]]). For such $f$ define

$$\int_u^v f \;:=\; \begin{cases} \text{the Darboux integral of } f \text{ over } [u,v] & \text{if } u < v, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } u = v, \\[2pt] -\displaystyle\int_v^u f & \text{if } u > v. \end{cases}$$

**There is nothing to check for consistency.** The three clauses are indexed by
the three cases of trichotomy, $u < v$, $u = v$ and $u > v$, which are mutually
exclusive and exhaustive; no pair of them ever applies to the same $(u,v)$. In
particular the first clause is untouched, so on $u < v$ this is the published
integral verbatim and every published theorem about it applies unchanged.

**The middle clause is a stipulation, not a computation.** It is *not* claimed
that $0$ is a value forced by the $u < v$ definition in any limiting sense; that
definition simply says nothing at $u = v$, and $\int_u^u f := 0$ is what is
written there. It is also unconditional: no hypothesis on $f$ beyond being
defined at $u$ is asked for, since the case $u = v$ never refers to a partition.

### The two consequences used throughout the page

**Antisymmetry, for every pair.** For all reals $u, v$ with $f$ integrable
between them,

$$\int_u^v f \;=\; -\int_v^u f .$$

Indeed if $u < v$ then $v > u$ and the third clause reads
$\int_v^u f = -\int_u^v f$, which rearranges to the display; if $u = v$ both
sides are $0$; and if $u > v$ the third clause is the display itself.

**Absolute values agree.** Consequently
$\bigl|\int_u^v f\bigr| = \bigl|\int_v^u f\bigr|$ for every such pair.

**An obligation recorded here and discharged elsewhere.** With this convention
the additivity identity

$$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f$$

holds for **every** arrangement of $u, v, w$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable, not only for $u < v < w$. That is a theorem and not part of this
definition; it is proved as the last clause of
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], and nothing on this page uses it before it
is proved there.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

derivations.claim: With $u=(v(y),0,0)$, [F2] gives $(u\cdot\nabla)u=0$ and $\Delta u=(v'',0,0)$; also $-\nabla p=(G,0,0)$ for $p=p_0-Gx$. Hence (NS) reduces to $0=G+\eta v''(y)$ and $\partial_yp=0$, i.e. $$v''(y)=-\frac{G}{\eta},\qquad p=p_0-Gx .$$ For part (b) with $p$ constant the first equation becomes $v''=0$.

(Poiseuille.) Apply [F3] to $w(y):=v(y)+\frac{G}{2\eta}y^2$, which satisfies $w''=0$ on $(0,h)$ and is continuous on $[0,h]$. Thus $w(y)=Ay+B$; the conditions $v(0)=v(h)=0$ give $B=0$ and $A=\frac{Gh}{2\eta}$, so $v(y)=\frac{Gy(h-y)}{2\eta}$, the stated profile; it is $C^\infty$ and satisfies both equations of step 1.1. Computing the flux, $$\int_0^hv=\frac{G}{2\eta}\Bigl(h\int_0^hy\,dy-\int_0^hy^2\,dy\Bigr)=\frac{G}{2\eta}\Bigl(\frac{h^3}{2}-\frac{h^3}{3}\Bigr)=\frac{Gh^3}{12\eta}.$$ If two profiles $v_1,v_2$ both solve $v''=-G/\eta$ with vanishing endpoints, their difference $w$ has $w''=0$ and $w(0)=w(h)=0$; by [F3], $w=0$.

(Couette.) For $v(y)=Vy/h$ we have $v''=0$, so step 1.1 is satisfied with constant $p$; the boundary values are $v(0)=0$ and $v(h)=V$. Finally $D_xu$ has the single nonzero entry $\partial_yu_1=V/h$ in row $1$, column $2$, while $\partial_xu_2=0$, so $D_xu\ne(D_xu)^{\mathsf T}$ when $V\ne0$: the antisymmetric part is nonzero and the flow is not irrotational by the definition above.
